source: CISA Secure Our World
content: Pause when a message uses urgent language, requests personal or financial information, or presents a suspicious sender or link. Treat these as reasons to verify rather than instructions to act.

metadata.source: CISA Secure Our World

source: CISA Secure Our World
content: Use the organization’s reporting mechanism for suspected phishing and then remove the message. Rapid reporting helps defenders investigate and protect other recipients.

metadata.source: CISA Secure Our World

source: NIST Small Business Cybersecurity: Phishing
content: Do not authenticate through an unsolicited link. Open the service from a known bookmark or manually entered official address and check for the expected domain before entering credentials.

metadata.source: NIST Small Business Cybersecurity: Phishing

source: NIST Small Business Cybersecurity: Phishing
content: Unexpected attachments should remain unopened until the sender and business need are independently confirmed. Maintain current endpoint protection because attachments may attempt to install malicious software.

metadata.source: NIST Small Business Cybersecurity: Phishing

source: FBI Business Email Compromise PSA
content: Verify any new or changed payment instruction through a trusted contact method already on file. Do not use a telephone number or reply address supplied only in the change request.

metadata.source: FBI Business Email Compromise PSA

source: FBI Internet Crime Report 2024
content: If a fraudulent transfer may have occurred, contact the financial institution immediately and follow the organization’s incident-response process. Preserve message and transaction evidence for reporting.

metadata.source: FBI Internet Crime Report 2024

source: NIST Cybersecurity Awareness: Recognizing and Reporting Phishing
content: An unusual or out-of-character request should create a deliberate pause. Confirm the request through a separate trusted route before clicking, paying, sharing data, or changing access.

metadata.source: NIST Cybersecurity Awareness: Recognizing and Reporting Phishing

source: NIST SP 800-171 Rev. 3
content: Security procedures still apply when a request claims to come from a senior executive, auditor, customer, or government authority. Escalation and verification protect both the employee and the claimed requester.

metadata.source: NIST SP 800-171 Rev. 3

source: NIST Small Business Cybersecurity: Phishing
content: End an unsolicited call that asks for credentials, authentication codes, remote access, sensitive information, or payment. Call the organization back using a verified directory or statement number.

metadata.source: NIST Small Business Cybersecurity: Phishing

source: FBI Internet Crime Report 2025
content: Do not use voice familiarity as the only approval factor. Apply the normal callback, dual-approval, and payment-control process even when a caller sounds like a known executive.

metadata.source: FBI Internet Crime Report 2025

source: NIST SP 800-63B-4
content: Never disclose a one-time authenticator output to a caller or message sender. Manually entered OTP values can be relayed by an impostor and are not phishing-resistant.

metadata.source: NIST SP 800-63B-4

source: NIST Small Business Cybersecurity: Phishing
content: For an unexpected text about a delivery, bank, password, or account, avoid the embedded link. Open the official app or independently locate the organization’s website and contact details.

metadata.source: NIST Small Business Cybersecurity: Phishing

source: CISA Implementing Number Matching
content: Deny and report any authentication request you did not initiate. An unexpected MFA prompt may mean the password was already entered successfully by another party.

metadata.source: CISA Implementing Number Matching

source: CISA Implementing Number Matching
content: Use number matching when push MFA is still required and train users to compare the number only during a sign-in they initiated. Investigate denied or bulk confirmation events.

metadata.source: CISA Implementing Number Matching

source: NIST SP 800-63B-4
content: Prefer cryptographic authentication such as WebAuthn or FIDO2 that binds the authentication to the legitimate verifier. Manual OTP entry and ordinary push approval do not provide the same phishing resistance.

metadata.source: NIST SP 800-63B-4

source: MITRE ATT&CK T1528
content: Before granting an application access, verify the publisher, business owner, and exact permissions. Reject unapproved requests for mail, files, contacts, offline access, or administrative scopes.

metadata.source: MITRE ATT&CK T1528

source: MITRE ATT&CK T1528
content: If malicious consent is suspected, report it so administrators can revoke access and refresh tokens, remove the application grant, and review activity performed under the token.

metadata.source: MITRE ATT&CK T1528

source: MITRE ATT&CK T1550.004
content: A password change alone may not end an attacker’s active web session. Incident response should revoke sessions and tokens and investigate sign-ins, devices, and application activity.

metadata.source: MITRE ATT&CK T1550.004

source: MITRE ATT&CK T1566.003
content: Treat unusual direct messages, scripts, file shares, payment requests, and authentication prompts as suspicious even when they come from an internal-looking account. Confirm through a ticket or second channel.

metadata.source: MITRE ATT&CK T1566.003

source: MITRE ATT&CK T1078
content: A legitimate account can be controlled by an attacker. Judge requests against normal workflow and independently verify unusual actions instead of relying only on the profile name or account history.

metadata.source: MITRE ATT&CK T1078

source: FBI IC3 QR Code PSA
content: Inspect the destination shown by the device before opening a QR link. Avoid codes that unexpectedly request payment or account login, and use the organization’s official application or typed website instead.

metadata.source: FBI IC3 QR Code PSA

source: FBI IC3 QR Code PSA
content: Check physical QR signs for overlays or tampering. When a code is associated with parking, payment, or access, verify the operator and destination through an official source.

metadata.source: FBI IC3 QR Code PSA

source: CISA ICT Supply Chain Risk Management Threat Scenarios
content: Do not connect found, mailed, or otherwise untrusted removable media to a work device. Give it to the designated security team for controlled analysis or disposal.

metadata.source: CISA ICT Supply Chain Risk Management Threat Scenarios

source: CISA Project Upskill: Protect Data on Devices
content: Encrypt approved removable media and the sensitive files it contains. Encryption limits disclosure if a small drive is lost or stolen.

metadata.source: CISA Project Upskill: Protect Data on Devices

source: MITRE ATT&CK T1557.004
content: Avoid open or unexpected wireless networks and do not dismiss certificate warnings. Confirm the correct network name with the venue or organization before connecting.

metadata.source: MITRE ATT&CK T1557.004

source: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3
content: Report suspected compromise promptly through the documented incident-response channel. Include what happened, the affected account or device, approximate time, and any action already taken.

metadata.source: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3

source: NIST SP 800-50 Rev. 1
content: Adapt learning activities to the risks and responsibilities of the audience. Finance, help desk, engineering, HR, and executives should practice the decisions they are likely to face.

metadata.source: NIST SP 800-50 Rev. 1

source: NIST SP 800-50 Rev. 1
content: Evaluate a learning program with defined outcomes and measures, then use results to improve content. Completion alone does not show that learners can recognize and respond to threats.

metadata.source: NIST SP 800-50 Rev. 1

source: NIST SP 800-161 Rev. 1
content: Use documented supplier contacts and approval paths when a vendor requests access, software changes, or payment changes. Treat deviations from the established relationship as a risk requiring review.

metadata.source: NIST SP 800-161 Rev. 1

source: CISA Use Strong Passwords
content: Use a password manager to generate and store unique passwords. Domain-aware autofill can also provide a useful warning when a counterfeit site does not match the saved login.

metadata.source: CISA Use Strong Passwords

source: NIST Small Business Cybersecurity: Phishing
content: After disclosing a password, notify the organization and change affected credentials immediately. Change reused passwords on other services and review account activity for unauthorized actions.

metadata.source: NIST Small Business Cybersecurity: Phishing

source: CISA StopRansomware Guide
content: Treat suspicious links and attachments as potential initial access for ransomware. Reporting an early phishing event can allow defenders to contain access before encryption or extortion occurs.

metadata.source: CISA StopRansomware Guide
